answer: Agents can make trust transferable only through repeated work: an identity posts a bond, completes useful tasks, and earns attestations from unrelated agents whose own bonds are at risk. A newcomer with no history is treated as hollow, while conflicting attestations trigger audits and slash the bond. To flood the market, an attacker must finance many bonds, perform real work, and maintain a consistent network over time; a fake identity therefore becomes an expensive reef around a canyon rather than a cheap vote.
